analysis.one_liner: Requires trucking companies to pay overtime wages after 40 hours a week.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced April 14, 2022 with 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican), it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never received a markup or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal wage law requires overtime pay after 40 hours a week, but commercial truck drivers have long been carved out of that requirement. This bill deletes that carve-out, so trucking companies would owe drivers time-and-a-half for hours worked past 40 in a week. The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial truck drivers — long-haul, regional, and delivery drivers who are paid hourly and routinely put in 50, 60, or more hours a week — would gain a federal right to time-and-a-half pay past 40 hours. Drivers' non-driving time (loading, waiting at docks, paperwork) currently counts as hours on the job without triggering overtime; this bill would change that.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly truck drivers working long weeks

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the motor-carrier exemption in Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the provision that has excluded commercial truck drivers from federal overtime protections since 1938.
Requires employers of commercial truck drivers to pay overtime for workweeks longer than 40 hours, matching the standard other covered workers already have.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies, which would owe overtime wages to drivers now exempt. Some of that cost could be passed along to shippers and, ultimately, to consumers through freight rates. Carriers that rely on long unpaid driver hours would see the biggest change.

drawbacks.text: Trucking is a thin-margin, high-turnover industry; the Department of Transportation already caps driving hours, so a large share of the new overtime pay would compensate waiting and loading time — a real cost to carriers that would show up in freight prices.

The exemption originally existed alongside strict federal regulation of carriers' rates and routes; after that regime was dismantled, critics of the bill argue carriers competing on price would face pressure to squeeze schedules elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a concrete wage increase for a workforce known for very long hours and unpaid wait time, and it applies to a single, clearly defined occupation rather than rewriting the whole law. The cost is higher labor costs for carriers in a competitive, low-margin industry, some of which would reach shippers and consumers. That is a real cost, but it is the same trade-off every overtime expansion makes, and drivers have been on the excluded side of it since 1938.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Levin (D-MI) introduced the bill on April 14, 2022, with seven original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day; that referral is the last action in the bill's history.
The bill ended the Congress with 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican) and never advanced out of committee or received a vote in the House or Senate.

The bill's sole substantive provision deletes the motor-carrier exemption from the Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime rules, making overtime pay mandatory for covered commercial truck drivers after 40 hours.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies are better off: the motor-carrier overtime exemption remains on the books, so carriers continue to owe drivers nothing beyond straight time past 40 hours a week. Drivers gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking companies still exempt from overtime

for.name: Andy Levin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with seven original cosponsors.

for.name: Jeff Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the sole Republican supporter.

against.name: Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled during the 117th Congress.

against.name: House Republican minority
against.role: 221 House Republicans not among the cosponsors
against.what_they_did: None of the 221 Republicans other than Van Drew cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the support needed to move it through a Democratically controlled committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 11 cosponsors split 10 Democrats to 1 Republican, and with no vote ever taken there is no roll-call record — the only measured partisan signal is the heavily one-sided cosponsor list.

industries.note: The industry's current exemption lets carriers pay straight time no matter how long a driver's week runs; the bill would have made hours past 40 cost time-and-a-half. Its financial interest in the exemption is the mirror image of drivers' interest in overtime.

industries.industry: Freight shippers and large retailers dependent on trucking
industries.note: Higher driver pay would likely raise freight rates, which shippers would partly pass to consumers. The public benefit — drivers earning overtime — and the public cost overlap in the same shipping prices.
